comparator.name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: Current route catalogue confirms 60 EC each year. In year three, the 30-EC taught and research allocation comprises one 10-EC exploration course, the 15-EC thesis project and 5 EC of professional impact. The separate 30-EC choice space remains open. Tutoring has no separate credit, and first-year tutoring is part of the positive study advice requirement. Current module admissions establish the sequence from first-year research and academic skills through second-year preparation and fieldwork, then the thesis, exploration and professional impact requirements.
components: Diversity and Development in a Sociological Perspective
Multivariate Analysis: from Data to Report
Personal and Professional Impact for Anthropologists
Genuine elective space preserved without inventing a minor, internship, exchange package or individual electives.

routeSelection.basis: The target is the generic bachelor. Both specialisations share the first year and the same total credit weight. Leiden presents People, Planet, Power first in its public programme structure, so this route is selected independently of UCR fit. Anthropology of Religion is the first option in the selected route’s 10-EC exploration group.

core: Cultural anthropology and development sociology: cultural meaning, diversity, identity, globalisation and social change
Ethnographic and qualitative research through fieldwork, participant observation, interviewing, ethics, writing and multimodal methods
Anthropological and sociological theory, comparative inquiry, quantitative analysis and an independent bachelor thesis
adjacent: People, Planet, Power: sustainability, development, ecology, politics and power
Media, Making, Movements: media, digital communities, social movements and creative or visual inquiry
Power, inequality, migration, citizenship and global connections
Contemporary public issues, exclusion and community responses to global change
questions: How do people create meaning, identity and social organisation across cultural contexts?
How do power, inequality, migration and development shape everyday experience?
How do ecological change, media technologies and social movements transform communities?

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: Classical and critical sociological theory connects solidarity, identity and social boundaries to class, race, gender and migration.
Historical inquiry into industrialisation, empire, migration and decolonisation supplies context for global cultural change.
Written argument, speeches, rhetorical analysis and storytelling develop tools for communicating social inquiry.
Interviews, ethnographic observation, documentary and visual methods, ethics and coding support empirical qualitative inquiry.
Primary sources, interviews and storytelling develop gender and sexuality history through North American cases and public history.
Comparative analysis of artefacts, production and identity supplies material-culture methods across Europe, Asia and Africa.
Moral theories and case argument provide ethical reasoning that can inform research responsibilities.
Critical, decolonial and intersectional social theory develops analysis of modernity, inequality and disciplinary exclusions.
Comparative historical cases investigate imperial ideology, governance, culture and legacies.
Comparative political analysis investigates institutions, participation and democratic change through operationalised measures.
Visual and audio evidence, archives and podcast production support study of racialisation and representation.
Theories and cases of international relations develop analysis of conflict, colonial relations and climate politics.
Western African visual traditions, museums and restitution connect material culture to regional histories and colonial power.
Stylistic analysis examines how linguistic choices, discourse and cognition shape interpretation.
Empirical research on social influence, prejudice and group processes adds behavioural perspectives on social life.
Civil-society theory and independent research address trust, public spheres, solidarity and social movements.
Political texts and essays develop analysis of authority, rights and normative accounts of social organisation.
Empirical coding of parliamentary amendments supports analysis of representation and institutions in Europe.
Human-rights law and political philosophy provide institutional and ethical context for inequality and citizenship.
Interdisciplinary research on conflict, identity, structural inequality and colonial legacies supports analysis of development and peace.
A substantial historical research paper develops question formulation, source criticism and methodological reasoning.
Documentary analysis and production connect visual evidence, representation, ethics and social context.
A research project compares literary interpretations using perspectives such as feminist, Marxist and minority approaches.
Planetary boundaries, uncertainty, modelling and physical principles explain material dimensions of environmental change.
Climate science, impacts, adaptation and mitigation provide context for climate justice and governance.
Waves, chemistry and materials work add scientific context for evaluating sustainability claims.
Cases of environmental governance and a Zeeland study relate institutions, participation, power and policy to collective environmental decisions.
Climate discourse and protest media analysis develop practical interpretation of public environmental arguments.
Environmental media analysis connects images, narratives, contested knowledge and public ecological debate.
Population and ecosystem ecology supplies an empirical basis for understanding ecological change.
Geochemical laboratory and modelling work explain environmental processes relevant to remediation and resource recovery.
Zeeland cases and an intervention proposal show how ecosystem-based design connects infrastructure and coastal adaptation.
Social movement theory and environmental justice cases examine contested transitions and civic engagement.
Close analysis of moving images, editing, sound and spectatorship supports visual interpretation and media history.
Museum and exhibition analysis examines curatorial framing and Eurocentric narratives through evidence-based art history.
Cleaning, analysing and visualising tabular, textual and spatial data in R gives practical quantitative tools.
Indigenous histories and collaborative public-history work explore representation, reciprocity and institutional violence.

alternatives.label: Culture, Society & Global Change
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum visibly combines culture, society, identity, global change and qualitative inquiry without implying a dedicated ethnographic fieldwork degree.
alternatives.concept: Study identity, inequality and cultural change through sociology, comparative history, politics and material culture. Qualitative inquiry, source criticism and documentary production give you different ways to investigate how people organise social life.
progression: The schedule has 24 distinct courses and 7 advanced courses. First-year personal and professional development, planned offerings and formal prerequisites pass the current workbook checks.

alternatives.label: Ecology, Communities & Global Change
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum combines social and cultural analysis with climate, sustainability, ecology and community responses to global change.
alternatives.concept: Study how communities and institutions respond to environmental change. Sociology, qualitative research and environmental governance connect with climate science, ecology, coastal adaptation and the public communication of environmental issues.
progression: The schedule has 24 distinct courses and 8 advanced courses. First-year personal and professional development, planned offerings and formal prerequisites pass the current workbook checks.
alternatives.distinctness: This route has 10 distinct courses compared with route 1, 10 distinct courses compared with route 3. Its central application and associated coursework distinguish it from both other routes.

alternatives.label: Visual Culture, Media & Social Inquiry
alternatives.concept: Study how images, institutions and media shape representation, identity and social action. Film, documentary production, museum studies and historical inquiry connect with sociology, qualitative methods and introductory text and spatial data analysis.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines cultural and social theory with film, media, visual inquiry, politics and data analysis; the label states those visible strands directly.
progression: The schedule has 24 distinct courses and 7 advanced courses. First-year personal and professional development, planned offerings and formal prerequisites pass the current workbook checks.
alternatives.distinctness: This route has 6 distinct courses compared with route 1, 10 distinct courses compared with route 2. Its central application and associated coursework distinguish it from both other routes.

blocks: Both introduce systematic theoretical study of society and social organisation, although Leiden provides a dedicated anthropology-and-sociology sequence.
Both situate cultural and social change historically and transnationally.
Both develop qualitative research design, interviewing, observation, analysis and interpretation; Leiden adds dedicated anthropological field practice.
Both examine modern social theory, diversity, inequality and changing social relations.
Both engage advanced social theory about power, inequality and contemporary societies.
The historical research paper develops a research question, source criticism and sustained argument. Leiden requires a distinct anthropology thesis.
Both use comparison to examine human communities and cultural difference, while archaeology and anthropology retain distinct methods.
UCR qualitative-methods study does not reproduce Leiden's separately credited ethnographic fieldwork component.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Leiden's multivariate-analysis component.
Both analyse states, citizenship, political institutions and power.
Governance cases connect institutions, power and collective environmental decisions. Leiden approaches these relations through anthropological political economy.
Rhetorical argument, writing and speaking provide partial preparation for disciplinary writing in anthropology.
Ethical argument supports reflection on research responsibilities. Leiden also teaches practical ethics and data handling for ethnography.
Both develop regionally grounded cultural analysis, though with distinct disciplinary objects and methods.
Both use mediated and visual forms to analyse and communicate social life.
Data preparation and visualisation in R are shared quantitative skills. Leiden teaches statistical analysis for anthropology and sociology.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Anthropology of Religion.
Academic reading and writing are distributed across the UCR programmes.
Both support reflection on academic development, professional identity and future pathways.
No single selected UCR course is presented as a direct counterpart to Leiden's specialisation-specific research preparation.
Leiden's genuine 30-EC elective space remains open and is not replaced by invented content.

selection.assessment: The broad route covers cultural difference, development, power and qualitative inquiry. The ecology route responds to the People, Planet, Power direction. The visual culture route responds to the media and representation strand of Media, Making, Movements, with digital ethnography remaining a gap. All three schedules are feasible and pairwise distinct.

notes.text: Leiden’s dedicated anthropology degree includes sequenced theory, ethnographic methods and fieldwork. At UCR, sociology, qualitative inquiry and related subjects offer a different combination of these interests.
Leiden reserves 30 EC in year three for approved elective choices, which can include a minor, exchange or eligible internship.

audience.programmeDescription: Leiden’s Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology degree studies cultural difference, inequality and social change through theory and field research. Students start with a common first year, then choose People, Planet, Power or Media, Making, Movements.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR routes connect sociology and qualitative research with global change, environmental governance or visual culture. They offer related study alongside gaps in dedicated anthropology theory, sequenced ethnographic fieldwork, digital ethnography and the Leiden thesis.

curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC shown include the People, Planet, Power specialisation, one 10-EC exploration choice and 30 EC of open elective space. Tutoring carries no separate credits. First-year tutoring is required for positive study advice.

componentNotes.y2-fieldwork: Pass the required first-year writing, research, ethics and statistics courses. Pass both research design contributions before starting the three-week January fieldwork. Tutorials, lectures and the closing conference are compulsory.
componentNotes.y2-research-preparation: The first-year research, ethics, writing and statistics requirements also apply to this preparation course.
componentNotes.y2-multivariate: Finish the Fieldwork NL research period and pass the required first-year courses before starting multivariate analysis.
componentNotes.y3-religion: One of the two 10-EC exploration options in this specialisation. Entry requires completion of the first year, Research Preparation, Fieldwork NL and both specialisation Key Issues courses.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: The 15-EC project combines thematic preparation, a proposal and an individual thesis. Entry requires the completed first year, Diversity and Power and at least one Key Issues course specific to the specialisation.
componentNotes.y3-impact: Complete the first- and second-year Academic Skills and Research Lab courses and Diversity and Power before registering.
componentNotes.y3-electives: The 30 EC may be used for approved electives, a minor, exchange or eligible internship arrangements. The allocation does not prescribe a particular package.
